quote: Despite recent advancements, large language models (LLMs) are known to produce factually incorrect output. [...] Sports reporting is one such domain, and in this paper, we investigate the factual accuracy of LLMs for generating NBA game summaries. This is a challenging text generation task [...] We evaluate factual and semantic errors [...] and attributes (e.g., scores, time, period, distance). We hypothesise that structuring the complex play-by-play data is important for producing factually accurate summaries [...] generate paragraph-style summaries from complete play-by-play data [...]

...We generate paragraph-style summaries from complete play-by-play data and compare three input structures: unstructured input with 13,000 tokens, row-structured input with 28,000 tokens, and JSON input with 70,000 to 80,000 tokens, producing summaries of 450 to 500 words...
we generate paragraph-style summaries from complete play-by-play data
datasets: NBA game play-by-play data from Basketball Reference

quote: ...We evaluate factual and semantic errors using a manual error-annotation protocol rather than automatic metrics such as ROUGE or BLEU...
...We will develop an LLM-as-Judge framework to complement costly manual evaluation by automatically assessing atomic factual claims against play‑by‑play input logs (future work)...

We manually annotated 3,312 errors across 180 play-by-play summaries generated for 30 NBA games [...] One of the authors manually annotated errors in all 180 generated summaries, and a second annotator independently annotated 9 summaries (5% of the dataset) to assess inter-annotator agreement. We provided detailed guidelines describing error categories, examples, and instructions for marking errors.

Annotators followed detailed guidelines describing error categories, examples, and instructions for marking errors at the token/phrase level.

We refined the annotation scheme  by splitting the original Word category into Word-objective (verifiable, fact-checkable wording errors) and Word-subjective (opinion-based wording not grounded in the play-by-play). We use seven categories in total: Number, Name, Word-objective, Word-subjective, Context, Not Checkable, and Other.
